meta.title: How One General Took Spain, and Why a King Gave It Back
meta.working_title: 36 Years of Franco: How Spain Fell Apart and Came Back
meta.device: A cracked Spanish flag hangs behind every act. The crack opens wider through the Republic and the war, is painted over in grey under Franco, and in the last act is repaired with a gold seam (kintsugi style) as democracy returns. The parchment map from parts 1 and 2 returns for the front lines.
meta.style: 2D dynamic, locked Village Painterly look: 6-head characters from the village-cast rig (smooth tapered limbs, detailed 4-finger hands, nose below the eye line), in 1920s-1980s dress (army uniforms, workers' overalls, militia caps, priests, 1970s suits). Highly detailed painted backgrounds with warm light and dynamic cast shadows: Madrid streets, Moroccan desert outposts, Barcelona barricades, Guernica's market square, a Castilian village, 1960s Costa del Sol beaches, the Spanish parliament chamber. Moving cameras, 3 to 5 parallax layers, characters acting in every shot, match-cut transitions. Violence is shown through shadows, smoke and aftermath, never gore. SFX under the VO; no music until combine.
meta.source: 'Ten Minute History: The Spanish Civil War and Francisco Franco' plus the 20th-century part of 'The Entire History of Spain', fact-checked; auto-caption names corrected.

shots.vo: On the twenty-third of February 1981, armed police burst into Spain's parliament during a live vote.
shots.visual: The parliament chamber; deputies in their seats; the doors fly open and civil guards in tricorn hats rush in.
shots.anim: Calm chamber, then the doors slam open; camera jolts.

shots.vo: Their leader climbed onto the speaker's platform with a pistol and fired at the ceiling. Most of the deputies dived under their seats.
shots.visual: Lieutenant Colonel Tejero with a moustache and pistol on the rostrum; plaster falls; deputies duck.
shots.anim: Muzzle flash, plaster dust drifts down; rows of empty seats.

shots.vo: Spain had been a democracy for less than four years. For the thirty-six years before that, it had been ruled by one general. Now the army was trying to bring those days back.
shots.visual: TV cameras in the chamber still rolling; a family at home watching on a small TV, frozen.
shots.anim: Push in on the TV screen in the living room.

shots.vo: That night, at about one in the morning, the king appeared on television in his army uniform. And what he said decided the fate of the country.
shots.visual: King Juan Carlos at a desk in uniform, under studio lights, facing the camera.
shots.anim: The studio light snaps on; slow push on his face.

shots.vo: To understand that night, you have to go back to a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Spaniards, and the general who won it.
shots.visual: The cracked flag fills the frame; the crack runs through it.
shots.anim: The crack splits wider with a sharp sound.

shots.visual: Title over a lone soldier's silhouette on a hill above a burning town.
shots.anim: Smoke drifts; the title fades up.

shots.vo: In 1898 Spain lost the last pieces of its empire to the United States. The country was poor, mostly farmers, and deeply split between rich landowners and the church on one side, and workers on the other.
shots.visual: A dusty Andalusian estate: a landowner on horseback; labourers bent over in the field.
shots.anim: The landowner rides past; workers straighten and watch him go.

shots.vo: The army looked for new glory in Morocco. In 1921, at Annual, Berber fighters wiped out a Spanish army. Thousands of soldiers died in days.
shots.visual: A Spanish desert outpost under attack; soldiers retreating across sand.
shots.anim: Heat haze; dust clouds; the outpost flag falls.

shots.vo: In 1923 General Miguel Primo de Rivera took power in a coup, with the king's blessing. He ruled as a dictator for seven years, then lost support and quit in 1930.
shots.visual: Primo de Rivera in uniform beside King Alfonso the Thirteenth on a balcony.
shots.anim: Crowd below; then the same balcony, empty.

shots.vo: The king was tainted by the dictatorship. In April 1931 republicans swept the big cities in local elections. Alfonso the Thirteenth left the country without abdicating.
shots.visual: Crowds in Madrid waving tricolour flags of red, yellow and purple; a royal car driving away at night.
shots.anim: Flags ripple; the car's tail lights fade.

shots.vo: Spain was a republic: the Second Spanish Republic. Its flag was red, yellow and purple.
shots.visual: The flag behind the act changes to the republican tricolour; the crack is still there.
shots.anim: The colour swap wipes down the flag.

shots.vo: The new government moved fast. A new constitution in 1931 separated church and state, gave women the vote, and promised land to poor farmers.
shots.visual: Parliament votes; a woman casts a ballot for the first time; a farmer is handed a deed.
shots.anim: Hands raise in a vote; the ballot drops into the box.

shots.vo: Manuel Azana, the prime minister, cut the army's officer corps, closed religious schools and gave Catalonia its own government.
shots.visual: Azana at a desk signing laws; an officer reads the news, angry; a priest watches a school door close.
shots.anim: Stamp, stamp, stamp; each reaction cuts in.

shots.vo: To the left these reforms were too slow. To the right, they were an attack on everything Spain stood for. Churches were burned. Strikes and street fights became normal.
shots.visual: A burning church at night; then a street brawl between workers and young men in blue shirts.
shots.anim: Flames; quick handheld shots of the brawl.

shots.vo: In 1933 the right won the election. In 1934 miners in Asturias rose up and declared a revolution. The government sent the army from Morocco. One of the generals directing it was Francisco Franco.
shots.visual: Miners with dynamite in a green mountain valley; then troops marching up the valley.
shots.anim: Mountain parallax; boots march; Franco studies a map in a tent.

shots.vo: In February 1936 the left united as the Popular Front and won. Political killings grew on both sides.
shots.visual: A crowd celebrating; then a shadowy street at night with posters torn down.
shots.anim: Cheering fades to silence as the camera drifts down the dark street.

shots.vo: On the thirteenth of July 1936, police officers took the monarchist leader Jose Calvo Sotelo from his home and shot him. Four days later, the army moved.
shots.visual: A police truck outside a Madrid apartment at night; a door opens.
shots.anim: Headlights; a door; cut to black.

shots.vo: On the seventeenth of July 1936, the army in Spanish Morocco rebelled. The plan was led by General Emilio Mola. The army's best troops were there.
shots.visual: A Moroccan barracks at dawn; officers hand out rifles; the flag is pulled down.
shots.anim: Bugle; flag descends; troops run to trucks.

shots.vo: Franco had been sent away to the Canary Islands to keep him out of trouble. A British plane, the Dragon Rapide, secretly flew him to Morocco to take command.
shots.visual: A small biplane lands on a desert airstrip; Franco steps down in a suit, then changes into uniform.
shots.anim: Propeller slows; match cut from suit jacket to uniform.

shots.vo: The plotters expected the government to give up in days. It did not. In Madrid and Barcelona, the new prime minister Jose Giral handed out rifles to workers and unions.
shots.visual: A Madrid street: crates of rifles opened; workers in overalls taking guns.
shots.anim: Crates crack open; hands reach in.

shots.vo: The coup half worked. Spain split in two. The rebels, who called themselves Nationalists, held the west and north. The Republic held Madrid, Barcelona and most of the industry.
shots.visual: The map splits into two colours with a jagged front line.
shots.anim: The line zigzags across; the flag's crack opens wide.

shots.vo: Franco's best troops were stuck in Africa, because the navy stayed loyal to the Republic. So German and Italian planes flew them across in one of the first big airlifts in history.
shots.visual: Trimotor planes over the Strait of Gibraltar; soldiers packed inside.
shots.anim: Planes cross the strait in a line; shadows on the water.

shots.vo: By October the other generals made Franco the head of state and commander. He called himself the Caudillo, the leader.
shots.visual: Generals in a room raise hands; Franco stands at the end of the table.
shots.anim: Hands go up one by one; Franco doesn't move.

shots.vo: The war became a test for the bigger war to come. Hitler and Mussolini sent planes, tanks and troops to Franco. Stalin sent weapons and advisers to the Republic.
shots.visual: Three shadowy figures behind a chessboard of Spain; pieces in their colours.
shots.anim: Hands move pieces onto the board.

shots.vo: Britain and France stayed out. But around thirty-five thousand volunteers from more than fifty countries came to fight for the Republic in the International Brigades.
shots.visual: A train full of young foreign volunteers in mixed clothes, singing.
shots.anim: Faces through windows; the train rushes past.

shots.vo: On the twenty-sixth of April 1937, a Monday, market day, German planes of the Condor Legion bombed the Basque town of Guernica for hours.
shots.visual: Guernica's market square with stalls and cattle; planes appear over the hills.
shots.anim: Peaceful market; a drone grows; people look up.

shots.vo: Much of the town was destroyed. Hundreds were killed. A few weeks later Pablo Picasso painted Guernica, and it became the most famous anti-war picture ever made.
shots.visual: Smoke over the ruined town; then Picasso in his studio in front of the huge grey canvas.
shots.anim: Smoke dissolves into the grey of the canvas.

shots.vo: The Republic was fighting itself as well. Communists, socialists, anarchists and others wanted different futures. In Barcelona in 1937 they fought each other in the streets.
shots.visual: Barcelona barricades: two left-wing militias firing at each other across a square.
shots.anim: Two sides, one street; dust from bullet hits.

shots.vo: The English writer George Orwell was there as a volunteer. A sniper shot him through the throat. He survived and wrote Homage to Catalonia.
shots.visual: A trench at dawn; a tall thin volunteer with a cigarette peers over; he falls back.
shots.anim: Quiet dawn; a crack; his cigarette drops.

shots.vo: Slowly, Franco's better-organised side won. Barcelona fell in January 1939, and Madrid at the end of March. On the first of April 1939, Franco declared the war over.
shots.visual: The Nationalist colour swallows the map; Barcelona, then Madrid flip.
shots.anim: Colour floods; the crack on the flag stops opening.

shots.vo: Estimates of the dead range from about three hundred and fifty thousand to half a million. Around half a million people fled to France.
shots.visual: A long line of refugees crossing snowy Pyrenees passes into France.
shots.anim: Snow falls; the line winds over the mountain.

shots.vo: Franco ruled alone. His party, the Falange, was the only legal one. Tens of thousands of Republicans were executed after the war, and many more were sent to prison camps.
shots.visual: A grey prison yard; prisoners in lines; a guard tower.
shots.anim: The colour drains from the frame to grey; the flag's crack is painted over in grey.

shots.vo: Catalan, Basque and Galician were pushed out of public life. Everything had to be Spanish, Catholic and obedient.
shots.visual: A school class reciting together under a crucifix and a portrait of Franco; a Catalan sign being painted over.
shots.anim: Brush paints over the sign; children recite in unison.

shots.vo: Then the Second World War began. In October 1940 Hitler met Franco at Hendaye, on the French border, to bring Spain into the war.
shots.visual: A train at a station platform; Hitler and Franco shake hands.
shots.anim: Steam from the train; the handshake in slow motion.

shots.vo: Franco asked for too much: French colonies in Africa, weapons and food. Hitler later said he would rather have three or four teeth pulled than go through that meeting again.
shots.visual: Hitler leaving the meeting, rubbing his jaw; Franco calm.
shots.anim: Hitler's hand rubs his jaw as the train door closes.

shots.vo: Spain stayed officially out of the war. But Franco sent about forty-five thousand volunteers, the Blue Division, to fight for Germany against the Soviet Union.
shots.visual: Spanish soldiers in blue shirts in the Russian snow.
shots.anim: Snow drifts across marching soldiers.

shots.vo: After 1945 Spain was shut out by the winners. Franco tried to make Spain feed itself without trade. It failed. The 1940s were called the years of hunger.
shots.visual: A ration queue in a village; a mother splitting one small loaf among her children.
shots.anim: Bread breaks; small hands reach.

shots.vo: Then the Cold War saved him. The Americans needed allies against communism. In 1953 they signed a deal for military bases in Spain in exchange for money. In 1955 Spain joined the United Nations.
shots.visual: An American jet lands at a Spanish airbase; an officer shakes Franco's hand.
shots.anim: Jet roars past; dollar signs drift over the map.

shots.vo: From 1959 Spain opened up its economy. Factories, cars and millions of tourists followed. They called it the Spanish miracle.
shots.visual: A 1960s Costa del Sol beach packed with tourists; a SEAT 600 car on the coast road; cranes building hotels.
shots.anim: Time-lapse: an empty beach fills with umbrellas and hotels.

shots.vo: In 1969 Franco named his successor: Prince Juan Carlos, grandson of the last king. He had been raised in Spain under Franco's eye. Everyone thought he would keep the system going.
shots.visual: Franco, old now, beside a tall young Juan Carlos at a ceremony.
shots.anim: Franco places a hand on his shoulder; Juan Carlos stays expressionless.

shots.vo: In December 1973 the Basque group ETA killed Franco's prime minister, Admiral Carrero Blanco. A bomb under a Madrid street threw his car over the roof of a church building.
shots.visual: A quiet Madrid street in the morning; a black car; a huge blast throws it upward.
shots.anim: Car drives over the spot; the street erupts; the car arcs over the roof.

shots.vo: On the twentieth of November 1975, Franco died. Two days later Juan Carlos became king.
shots.visual: A hospital room with drawn curtains; then Juan Carlos sworn in before parliament.
shots.anim: Curtain closes; match cut to the parliament doors opening.

shots.vo: He had sworn to keep Franco's system. Instead he picked a young Francoist official, Adolfo Suarez, as prime minister, and together they took it apart from the inside.
shots.visual: Juan Carlos and Suarez in a quiet office at night, papers between them.
shots.anim: Two men lean in; the lamp light warms.

shots.vo: They persuaded Franco's own parliament to vote itself out of existence. In April 1977 they legalised the Communist Party, which shocked the army.
shots.visual: Old Francoist deputies voting; one by one their seats empty out; posters of new parties go up outside.
shots.anim: Seats empty; posters slap onto a wall.

shots.vo: In June 1977 Spain held its first free election in forty-one years. In 1978 a new constitution made Spain a democracy with a king who reigns but does not rule, and gave Catalonia and the Basque Country their own governments.
shots.visual: Long queues of voters of all ages outside a village school; ballots dropping into a glass box.
shots.anim: The cracked flag starts to fill with a gold seam.

shots.vo: Which brings us back to February 1981. While the gunmen held parliament, tanks rolled into the streets of Valencia.
shots.visual: Back in the parliament chamber; deputies on the floor; tanks in Valencia at night.
shots.anim: Hard cut from the chamber to tank tracks on wet street.

shots.vo: The plotters thought the king would back them. Instead, at a quarter past one in the morning, he went on television and ordered the army to support the constitution.
shots.visual: The king on the family's TV screen; the family slowly stands up.
shots.anim: Push from the TV to the family's faces.

shots.vo: By the next morning the coup was over. The gunmen walked out of the parliament and surrendered.
shots.visual: Dawn; civil guards leave the parliament through a window, hands empty.
shots.anim: Morning light; the doors open; deputies step out.

shots.vo: Spain joined NATO in 1982 and the European Community in 1986. A country that had spent forty years cut off became one of Europe's most visited places.
shots.visual: Modern Spain: Barcelona's 1992 Olympic stadium with fireworks.
shots.anim: Fireworks bloom; the gold seam completes across the flag.

shots.vo: From Tariq's seven thousand men in 711, to the Alhambra in 1492, to an empire of silver, to a civil war and a dictator. Spain broke apart again and again. And each time, it put itself back together.
shots.visual: Quick recap montage in the painterly style: Gibraltar, the Alhambra, a galleon, Guernica, the parliament.
shots.anim: Five match cuts, one per era, ending on the repaired flag.

hooks: You've never seen this: in 1981 gunmen took Spain's parliament live on TV, and one man in a uniform decided what happened next.
You think democracies die slowly. Spain's almost died in one night, on live TV.

Franco Ruled Spain for 36 Years. Then His Chosen King Betrayed Him.

fixes: Auto-caption names fixed: Azaña, Alcalá-Zamora, Berenguer, Aznar (Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar), Mola, Calvo Sotelo, Lerroux, Asturias, Condor Legion, José Giral, autarky, Ceuta and Melilla, Carrero Blanco, Francoist.
Women's suffrage was in the 1931 constitution; women first voted in a general election in Nov 1933. Script says the constitution 'gave women the vote'.
Annual (July 1921): Spanish dead commonly estimated 8,000 to 13,000; script says 'thousands'.
Alfonso XIII left Spain on 14 April 1931 without formally abdicating.
Calvo Sotelo was killed on 13 July 1936 by Assault Guards and socialist militants; script says 'police officers'.
Franco flew from the Canaries on the Dragon Rapide (a British plane chartered in London) on 18-19 July 1936.
Barcelona fell 26 January 1939 (transcript says February); Madrid 28 March 1939; war declared over 1 April 1939.
Civil war death toll estimates range widely (about 350,000 to 500,000); script gives the range.
Guernica: transcript says 'killing five percent of its population'; the toll is disputed (from about 150 to several hundred). Script says 'hundreds'.
International Brigades: about 35,000 to 40,000 volunteers from more than 50 countries.
Spain was 'non-belligerent' from 1940 to 1943; Blue Division about 45,000 men in total.
Hendaye 23 Oct 1940; Hitler's 'three or four teeth' remark is reported by Mussolini's foreign minister Ciano / in Hitler's later talk; script presents it as 'Hitler later said'.
Post-war executions: historians estimate tens of thousands (often cited as around 50,000). Script says 'tens of thousands'.
Pact of Madrid 1953; UN membership December 1955; Stabilisation Plan 1959.
Juan Carlos named successor July 1969; Franco died 20 Nov 1975; Juan Carlos proclaimed king 22 Nov 1975.
Carrero Blanco killed 20 Dec 1973; the car was thrown over the Jesuit residence/church building.
Communist Party legalised 9 April 1977; election 15 June 1977; constitution ratified 6 Dec 1978.
23-F: Tejero entered at about 18:23 on 23 Feb 1981; king's broadcast at about 1:14 am on 24 Feb; tanks in Valencia under General Milans del Bosch.
cuts: No sponsor read. Dropped the 'book recommendations' outro and the Ifni War and Equatorial Guinea details to keep the story tight. Franco 'not really fascist' framing from the source replaced with plain facts about the regime.
